variants.name: Rack middleware stack (Rack::Builder#use)
variants.implementation_notes: Rack is Ruby's pipeline contract: a middleware is any object whose `call(env)` either forwards by calling the next application it was constructed with or returns its own `[status, headers, body]` triple to stop the chain; `Rack::Builder#use` (and `config.middleware.use` in Rails) composes them in declaration order, so the successor is injected at build time. Rack::Lint exists to verify compliance, which turns the handle-or-forward contract from convention into something testable.
pitfalls: Middleware must not call each on the response body except through a wrapper; the Rack SPEC requires the original body to be closed exactly once.
A middleware that swallows exceptions or returns a body without close() breaks downstream servers; verify with Rack::Lint.
Rails inserts default middleware around yours, so position new links with insert_before/insert_after instead of assuming an index.

variants.name: Hand-written successor chain
variants.implementation_notes: Outside web servers the classic structure is written directly: a base handler with a `successor` accessor and a `handle(request)` method, concrete handlers that handle or delegate, and an explicit terminal handler. Ruby's duck typing means no interface is required - the contract is the method name - which shortens the code but also removes any reminder that every link must answer the request, so the terminal handler and the return convention have to be documented.
variants.code_sketch:
class Handler
  attr_accessor :successor

  def handle(request)
    return :unhandled unless successor
    successor.handle(request)
  end
end
pitfalls: Without a documented contract, a handler that forgets to call successor drops the request silently.
attr_accessor on a shared chain invites runtime rewiring from any thread; freeze the chain after assembly.
method_missing-based forwarding turns a missing handler into a NoMethodError far from the chain's assembly site.
